The universe is constantly changing. The challenge isn't simply observing those changes—it's understanding which ones matter, why they happen, and what the evidence truly tells us.

HEIMDALL is an interactive, evidence-first astronomical investigation platform built around NASA's SPHEREx mission. It transforms complex multi-wavelength observations into an accessible scientific journey, allowing users to explore the sky across space, time, and wavelength, investigate unusual signals, and examine the evidence behind possible explanations.

Rather than treating every anomaly as a discovery, HEIMDALL connects detection and pattern analysis with astronomical measurements, uncertainty, cross-catalog context, and competing scientific hypotheses. Its goal is to make rigorous investigation approachable without sacrificing scientific integrity.

Rishabh developed the Python-based investigation engine, data-processing workflows, analytical algorithms, and interactive frontend, including the machine-learning experimentation. details:
HEIMDALL — From Observation to Understanding

The universe does not announce its discoveries. It leaves clues.

A faint object shifts against the stars. A familiar source changes brightness. An unusual pattern emerges across wavelengths. Each observation might reveal something important—or simply reflect noise, instrumental effects, or incomplete data.

HEIMDALL was built to investigate that difference.

What We Developed

HEIMDALL is an interactive, evidence-first astronomical research workbench designed around NASA's SPHEREx mission. Rather than presenting astronomical observations as disconnected images, charts, and catalogs, it brings spatial, temporal, and spectral information together into a continuous scientific investigation.

The platform allows users to navigate the sky, inspect observational coverage, explore SPHEREx's 102 wavelength channels, compare observations across time, and investigate sources that exhibit potentially interesting behavior.

Its central philosophy is simple: detecting something unusual is only the beginning of understanding it.

How HEIMDALL Works

HEIMDALL connects several stages of astronomical investigation:

1. Explore the sky. Users navigate an interactive sky map, search coordinates or known astronomical objects, and inspect available observational coverage before beginning an investigation.

2. Discover patterns. The investigation engine examines astronomical measurements for potentially meaningful behavior, including positional motion, brightness variability, wavelength-dependent differences, and anomalous signals. Statistical techniques and machine-learning experimentation support the broader detection framework.

3. Investigate across dimensions. Users can examine wavelength-ordered observations, navigate available epochs, compare compatible images, and explore how evidence changes across space, time, and wavelength.

4. Question the evidence. HEIMDALL considers measurement uncertainty, observational limitations, source identification, and alternative explanations. A suspicious signal may reflect genuine astrophysical behavior, but it may also arise from noise, blending, incomplete coverage, or instrumental effects.

5. Trace the conclusion. Investigations preserve connections to measurements, methods, source products, and provenance, helping users understand not only what the system reports but why.

This approach makes HEIMDALL more than a visualization interface. It is designed as a bridge between astronomical data, computational analysis, and human scientific reasoning.

Technology and Development

HEIMDALL combines a Python-based scientific backend with an interactive browser-based frontend.

The scientific engine uses Python and astronomical data-processing techniques for observation retrieval, coordinate handling, astrometry, photometry, statistical analysis, uncertainty assessment, and investigation workflows. It integrates with public astronomical data services, including NASA/IPAC IRSA and relevant reference catalogs such as Gaia and CatWISE.

The frontend brings these capabilities into an interactive environment through sky navigation, coordinated visualizations, wavelength exploration, temporal comparison, and evidence inspection.

The project also incorporates automated testing, reproducibility checks, network-resilience mechanisms, and documented scientific limitations.

Rishabh led the software engineering, Python investigation engine, frontend development, analytical algorithms, and machine-learning experimentation. Amy focused on the astronomical research, scientific foundations, and evaluation of the accuracy, reliability, and limitations of the project's scientific interpretations.

What Makes HEIMDALL Different?

Many astronomical tools help users access observations or visualize data. HEIMDALL focuses on the questions that follow:

What changed? Is the change meaningful? What explanations are consistent with the evidence? What remains unknown?

Its distinguishing approach is the integration of interactive exploration with evidence-based investigation.

Rather than hiding uncertainty behind a confident-looking result, HEIMDALL makes scientific limitations part of the experience. Rather than requiring users to navigate disconnected tools, it aims to keep the observational context, analytical results, and supporting evidence connected.

The system is also designed to serve different levels of expertise. A curious beginner can explore an accessible explanation, while a more experienced investigator can examine measurements, uncertainties, and competing hypotheses.

Scientific Responsibility

One of our most important design decisions was to distinguish a detected anomaly from a confirmed discovery.

Astronomical observations are affected by sensitivity limits, incomplete wavelength coverage, source confusion, measurement errors, and differences between observation epochs. These factors must be considered before interpreting unusual behavior.

HEIMDALL therefore emphasizes traceability, reproducibility, uncertainty, and the ability to acknowledge when the available evidence cannot support a conclusion.

The project uses known astronomical targets as investigation checkpoints and combines automated software tests with scientific validation workflows. Live-data availability and incomplete validation remain explicitly documented rather than being presented as successful discoveries.

Intended Impact

SPHEREx is opening an extraordinary new perspective on the infrared universe. But the scientific value of a survey is not determined only by how much information it collects. It also depends on how effectively people can explore, interpret, and question that information.

HEIMDALL aims to make this process more accessible to students, educators, citizen scientists, and researchers.

For newcomers, it offers an approachable way to engage with real astronomical evidence. For experienced users, it provides a connected environment for inspecting observations and investigating potential changes.

Our ambition is not to replace astronomers or automate scientific discovery into a single score. It is to build a tool that helps people ask better questions, examine stronger evidence, and recognize the limits of what they know.

Because the future of astronomical exploration is not simply about seeing more of the universe. It is about understanding what we see—and knowing when to look closer.
